clue.text: Risky food passed round not later than end of Christmas — mind the sprouts!

indicators.note: something passed round something else encircles it, so one piece wraps about the other

parts.note: bait is food offered to an animal at its peril
by Friday means not later than Friday

indicators.note: the end of a word is its closing letter, the only one kept

parts.note: the final letter of Christmas

explanation.surface: A festive warning about dodgy dinner leftovers and the dreaded Brussels sprouts on the plate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sprouts' looks like the Christmas vegetable, but it means children, young offshoots of the family; bait is risky food because the fish that eats it gets caught.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprouts is a playful word for small children, and to look after children while parents are out is exactly what this hyphenated verb describes.

clue.text: Cook sounds like an ass, did you say?

indicators.note: asking whether you heard right points to a word that is only being said, not spelt

parts.note: a donkey's call is a bray, so making that noise is braying

explanation.surface: Someone mocking a chef who honks like a donkey, then checking they heard right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sounds like' tempts you to read a homophone signal, but it is part of the wordplay: what an ass does is BRAYS, and 'did you say' is the real sound-alike signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To braise is to cook meat or vegetables slowly in a covered pot with a little liquid, a standard kitchen method.

clue.text: Great work and promotions for cleaners

indicators.note: this conjunction simply adds one thing to the next, so pieces sit side by side

parts.note: brill is informal British slang for brilliant or great
OP is short for opus, a musical work
adverts promote products

explanation.surface: A firm praising its staff and handing out promotions to the cleaning team.
explanation.walkthrough: BRILL + OP + ADS runs on as BRILLO PADS. Brillo pads are a British brand of soapy steel-wool scourers.
explanation.definitionFit: These soap-filled wire-wool pads are household scourers for scrubbing pans, so they are kitchen cleaners by brand name.

clue.text: Weapons manufacturer in cahoots in the end with writer

indicators.note: going along with something places it alongside, so pieces join in sequence
at the end of a word sits its final letter, which is all that is kept

parts.note: the final letter of cahoots
a wordsmith is a skilled writer

explanation.surface: An arms dealer secretly colluding with an author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In cahoots' reads as a phrase meaning in league, but 'in' is the link and only the last letter of cahoots is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A smith who forges blades makes swords, the classic hand weapons, so he is a maker of arms.

clue.text: Where water might be taken, not quite drier

indicators.note: falling just short means the final letter is lost

parts.note: a bucket is carried to a well to draw water

explanation.surface: Musing about where water goes, and comparing something to something only slightly less wet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drier' looks like a comparative adjective, but it is a noun: a thing that dries. TO WELL loses its last L.
explanation.definitionFit: A cloth used to rub off moisture after washing or bathing is a device that dries you.

clue.text: Stupid effin' old man's twittering nonsense?

indicators.note: this preposition puts one piece inside another

parts.note: cove is old British slang for a man or chap

indicators.note: something stupid is muddled, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: the clipped swear word read as two parts, EFF followed by the word in, whose second part is the insertion signal

explanation.surface: A rude jibe at an elderly man spouting rubbish on Twitter.
explanation.walkthrough: The trick is splitting 'effin’' in two so that its tail becomes the insertion signal. Covfefe was Donald Trump's garbled 2017 tweet.
explanation.definitionFit: The word was an infamous meaningless typo posted on Twitter, so it is literally gibberish from a tweet, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Nude dancing in ring with a marigold

indicators.note: going along with something places it alongside, so pieces join in sequence
this preposition puts one piece inside another

parts.note: to ring someone is to call them on the phone

indicators.note: dancing moves around, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written

explanation.surface: A naked dancer cavorting in a circle holding a flower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' suggests a circle or the letter O, but it is the verb meaning to phone someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Calendula is the botanical genus name of the pot marigold, so the two are the same garden flower.

clue.text: Pence under vainglorious egomanic, evidently all kicking off — for him previously?

definitions.text: Pence under vainglorious egomanic, evidently all kicking off — for him previously?

indicators.note: in a down entry, being below something places it after it
every word starting off means each one gives up only its opening letter

parts.note: opening letters of these three words
P is the abbreviation for pence

explanation.surface: Mike Pence serving under a boastful, self-obsessed boss, and everything kicking off.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: the vainglorious egomaniac is Trump, and Pence was his vice president during the first term, hence 'previously'.
explanation.definitionFit: Veep is informal American slang for vice president, the office Mike Pence held under Donald Trump from 2017 to 2021.

clue.text: Serialised copies I'd adapted

indicators.note: something adapted has been altered into a new form, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A writer saying the copies they adapted came out in instalments.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in I'd is ignored; its letters I and D join the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A story told in instalments, like a television drama broadcast in parts, comes in episodes.

clue.text: Charger where mobile finally rested, one having left phone plugged in

indicators.note: at last means the closing letter is the one kept

parts.note: the final letter of mobile

indicators.note: a plug goes inside a socket, so one piece is inserted into another

parts.note: leant against a wall means rested on it

indicators.note: something that has departed is gone, so those letters are removed

parts.note: taken as written, before part of it departs
taken as written, the letters that leave

explanation.surface: Tracking down where a phone was left charging, with one plugged into the wall.
explanation.walkthrough: Charger, mobile and phone all suggest gadgets; a charger here is an animal that charges. PH plugs into E + LEANT.
explanation.definitionFit: An elephant is a huge animal that may rush at intruders, so it is a creature that charges.

clue.text: Could I be fit for comrade?

parts.note: a question asking 'am I?'
go as an adjective means working properly, as in all systems go

explanation.surface: Someone wondering whether they are good enough to be a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: The question 'Could I be fit?' is rephrased as 'Am I go?', using go in its sense of ready and in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Amigo is the Spanish word for friend, used in English for a pal or companion.

clue.text: Gluttonous beast, cruciverbalist after missing starter opens booze

indicators.note: something that splits another apart sits inside it

parts.note: wine is a kind of alcoholic drink

indicators.note: lacking the opening course means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: a crossword enthusiast solves puzzles

explanation.surface: A greedy crossword fan, having skipped the starter, cracks open the drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' reads as a first course of a meal, but it means the first letter. A cruciverbalist is a crossword enthusiast.
explanation.definitionFit: The wolverine's other common name is glutton, from its reputation for eating ravenously, so it is a famously greedy animal.

clue.text: Fellow has blueprint written in day for rocket, say

indicators.note: words written in a space sit within it

parts.note: SAT is the abbreviation for Saturday

indicators.note: possessing something keeps it alongside, so pieces follow one another

parts.note: a lad is a young fellow
a blueprint is a design or plan

explanation.surface: An engineer drafting plans for a space rocket on a given day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocket' suggests spaceflight; it is the peppery leafy green also called arugula in America.
explanation.definitionFit: Rocket is a peppery leaf eaten raw in mixed greens, so it is one example of a plant grown for salads.

clue.text: Drop a log on head of hungry bear

indicators.note: placed on something means set next to it, so pieces join

parts.note: dropping a log is crude slang for defecating

indicators.note: the head of something is its top, so the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of hungry

explanation.surface: A camper dropping a log on a hungry bear's head to fend it off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop a log' paints firewood or a falling branch, but it is lavatory slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Winnie-the-Pooh is A. A. Milne's honey-loving teddy, the most famous fictional bear in children's books.

clue.text: A lovely fish — is that not quite right?

definitions.note: a question whose answer is the solution, describing an angle of less than ninety degrees

parts.note: taken as written
cute means sweetly attractive
to angle is to fish with a rod and line

explanation.surface: Someone admiring a pretty fish, then doubting whether it is quite right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish' is a verb here, not a creature. 'Not quite right' plays on a right angle of ninety degrees.
explanation.definitionFit: Any angle smaller than ninety degrees falls short of a right angle, so it is almost but not entirely right.

clue.text: See 17 Down
Nordic jewel's back, and pearl lost

indicators.note: the back of a word is its rear end, so only the closing letter is used

parts.note: the final letter of jewel

indicators.note: something lost has gone astray, so these letters wander into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A Scandinavian whose jewel has come back but whose pearl has gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jewel's back' looks like a jewel returning; it is just the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Lapland is the far northern region of Scandinavia and Finland, so a native of it is a northern European, a Nordic person.

clue.text: See 22 Across
Uncomfortable in bust after minor design failure

indicators.note: coming later in time means placed later in sequence

parts.note: a ward is a minor under the care of a guardian

indicators.note: something bust is broken, so these letters are smashed and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A young person squirming because a badly designed top fails across the chest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' sits in the picture as a chest but signals the jumble. The phrase was coined after Janet Jackson's 2004 Super Bowl costume mishap.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a euphemism for clothing that slips and exposes the wearer, a failure of the costume's tailoring.

clue.text: Possible requirement when cut in trade reversed, better finally

indicators.note: turned around means read in the opposite direction

parts.note: a sale is a commercial trade
to top someone is to better them
last of all means finally

explanation.surface: Talk of cuts in trade being reversed and things getting better in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' sounds economic but means a wound, and 'finally' is a word to translate, not a last-letter signal. Elastoplast is a British brand of sticking plaster.
explanation.definitionFit: When you nick your skin, an adhesive bandage strip is what you might need, so this brand is a possible need after a wound.

clue.text: A Kazakh__ capital in actuality?

parts.note: surface reading: name a city that serves as Kazakhstan's seat of government
setter's reading: the city's name is literally the Kazakh word meaning capital

explanation.walkthrough: The underline marks the Kazakh word for 'capital'; the capital city's name is literally that word.
explanation.definitionFit: Kazakhstan's capital has a name meaning simply 'capital city' in the Kazakh language, so it is a capital both in fact and in name.

clue.text: Constitutional guarantees ultimately something of a myth?

indicators.note: in the end means only the closing letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of guarantees
a troll is a creature from Norse myth and folklore

explanation.surface: A sceptic wondering whether constitutional rights are really just a myth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constitutional' suggests law, but it is a noun: a walk taken for the health.
explanation.definitionFit: A constitutional is an old-fashioned word for a leisurely walk taken for health, so it is a gentle walk.

clue.text: See 2 Down
Steps taken after worker gets near figure in minor skirmish

indicators.note: something taken after comes later, so it is placed at the end of the sequence

parts.note: a hand is a manual worker, as in farmhand
to bag something is to get or claim it
at the door means near it
ten is a number
paces are steps

explanation.surface: A labourer pacing out the distance before a petty scrap with a rival.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang 'handbags' is a petty scuffle with more posturing than punches; the phrase mocks a duel at ten paces.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a trivial, mostly harmless squabble, like a mock duel with handbags as weapons, so it is a small fight.

clue.text: Store soaked up

indicators.note: in a down entry, going upward means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: to tope is an old word meaning to drink heavily

explanation.surface: A storeroom that has been flooded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soaked up' reads as absorbed, but 'soaked' alone means boozed, and 'up' flips it.
explanation.definitionFit: A depot is a warehouse or storehouse where goods are kept, so it is a place for storage.

clue.text: Screwing originally, what snooker player would do in type of competition

indicators.note: at its origin means the opening letter alone is taken

parts.note: the first letter of screwing
snooker players sink balls into pockets, called potting

explanation.surface: A snooker commentator describing a screw shot, the backspin that makes the cue ball draw back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screwing' is snooker jargon for backspin, which suits the picture, but only its first letter counts. Spot the ball is a British newspaper contest where you mark a hidden ball's position in a photo.
explanation.definitionFit: The game is a newspaper puzzle in which entrants guess where a ball has been erased from a sports photo, so it is a competition.

clue.text: Tripped during competition — in bits

indicators.note: something happening during an event falls within it

parts.note: a cup is a knockout competition
to trip is to skip or hop lightly

explanation.surface: A player tripping up mid-tournament and ending up in pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tripped' suggests stumbling, but here it is the light dancing step.
explanation.definitionFit: Food or anything else that has been cut into small pieces with a knife ends up in fragments.

clue.text: Initially gung-ho, unusually aggressive, now official is dropping matter

indicators.note: at the outset means only the opening letters are used

parts.note: first letters of the five words that follow

explanation.surface: A gung-ho, belligerent official suddenly dropping a case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dropping matter' sounds like abandoning an issue; it is the stuff of droppings.
explanation.definitionFit: Guano is the accumulated excrement of seabirds and bats, valued as fertiliser, so it is bird droppings.

clue.text: Safeguard rank defending lieutenant

indicators.note: defenders surround what they protect, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: rank as an adjective means utter or sheer, as in rank stupidity
LT is the military abbreviation for lieutenant

explanation.surface: Soldiers in their ranks protecting their officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rank' looks like a military row, but it is the adjective meaning utter.
explanation.definitionFit: To shelter someone is to protect them from harm, so the verbs are synonyms.
